a: Put a knife to your throat
p: The Hebrew tells the greedy guest to put a knife to his throat; the Greek tells him to reach out his hand.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate ("statue cultrum in gutture tuo")
readings.en: and put a knife in your throat
readings.plain: Put a knife to your throat

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπίβαλλε τὴν χεῖρά σου εἰδὼς ὅτι τοιαῦτά σε δεῖ παρασκευάσαι
readings.en: and put out your hand, knowing that you must provide such things
readings.plain: Reach out your hand, knowing you must lay on such a meal yourself;

why: The Hebrew is vivid but clear, and the Latin agrees with it. The Greek seems to have read the rare word sakkin, 'knife', differently or to have rewritten the hard image, and it moves 'if you are greedier' into 23:3.
b: The Greek of 23:1–3 reads as a whole: "If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, consider wisely what is set before you, and put out your hand, knowing that you must provide such things; but if you are greedier, do not desire his dishes, for these belong to a false life." It turns the warning into etiquette: eat, but remember you will have to return the meal.

a: if you are a man of large appetite
t: Moved to the next verse in the Greek
p: The Greek has no second line here; it begins 23:3 with 'but if you are greedier'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate
readings.en: if you are a master of appetite
readings.plain: if you are a man of large appetite

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees; the line appears at the start of 23:3
readings.en: (but if you are greedier, at the start of 23:3)

why: The Hebrew keeps the condition with the knife command; the Greek, having turned the knife into a hand, moved the condition into the next verse.

a: Buy truth, and do not sell it:
t: A verse the Greek does not have
p: The Old Greek has no 23:23; it goes straight from 23:22 to 23:24.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate (veritatem eme)
readings.en: buy truth and do not sell (it)
readings.plain: Buy truth, and do not sell it:

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees; the whole verse is absent
readings.en: (no verse 23)

why: Every Hebrew manuscript has the verse, and the Latin translates it. Whether the Greek translator's Hebrew lacked it or he left it out cannot be settled; the note at this verse gives both views.

a: For a prostitute is a deep pit,
p: The Hebrew has 'prostitute' (zonah); the Greek has 'a strange house', which may reflect zarah, 'strange woman'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate (fovea enim profunda est meretrix)
readings.en: for a deep pit is a prostitute
readings.plain: For a prostitute is a deep pit,

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.orig: πίθος γὰρ τετρημένος ἐστὶν ἀλλότριος οἶκος
readings.en: for a strange house is a jar with holes
readings.plain: For a strange house is a jar full of holes,

why: The Hebrew is clear and pairs the prostitute with the foreign woman of the next line. The Greek 'strange' (allotrios) may show that the translator read zarah, the 'strange woman' of 2:16 and 22:14, for zonah, letters that look alike; his 'jar with holes' is his own image.

a: For he is the kind who keeps score inside.
t: Keeping score, or swallowing a hair?
p: The Hebrew describes a host who counts the cost; the Greek reads the same letters as 'hair'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for as he reckons in himself, so is he
readings.plain: For he is the kind who keeps score inside.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.orig: ὃν τρόπον γὰρ εἴ τις καταπίοι τρίχα οὕτως ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει
readings.en: for as if someone were to swallow a hair, so he eats and drinks
readings.plain: For he eats and drinks like someone choking down a hair.

why: The Hebrew is hard but makes sense in context: the stingy host reckons up every mouthful. The Greek read the consonants שער as se'ar, 'hair', which also fits the 'throw up' of 23:8.
b: The Hebrew sha'ar ('reckon') is rare, and the line has troubled translators. The Greek's hair in the throat is close to Amenemope's picture of rich food as "a storm in the gullet" that the body throws out (see the note at 23:8), and some modern scholars think the Greek or a repointed Hebrew is closer to the original image. The Greek also adds a line: "Do not bring him in to yourself, and do not eat your bread with him." The KJV's "as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" follows the Hebrew but takes it out of context (see the note).

t: Keep my ways, or delight in them?
p: The written Hebrew says 'take delight in my ways'; the reading tradition says 'keep my ways'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); Greek (τηρείτωσαν, 'let them keep'); Latin Vulgate (custodiant)
readings.en: let them keep (watch over)
readings.plain: keep watch on my ways

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Ketiv (the written consonants); followed by some modern translations
readings.en: let them take pleasure in
readings.plain: take delight in my ways

why: The Qere is supported by the Greek and the Latin and matches the language of 'keeping' ways elsewhere in Proverbs (2:8; 2:11). The Ketiv differs by two letters swapped (רצ / צר) and also makes good sense.

a: Do not stare at the wine as it turns red
t: A different verse in the Greek
p: The Greek has 'Do not get drunk with wine', the very words Paul uses in Ephesians 5:18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate
readings.en: do not look at wine when it shows itself red
readings.plain: Do not stare at the wine as it turns red

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees (Swete's Vaticanus has ἐν οἴνοις, 'with wines')
readings.orig: μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ ἀλλὰ ὁμιλεῖτε ἀνθρώποις δικαίοις
readings.en: do not get drunk with wine, but talk with righteous people, and talk as you walk
readings.plain: Do not get drunk on wine; spend your time with righteous people instead, and talk with them as you walk,

why: The Hebrew is the original; the Greek is a free paraphrase that turns a warning about the look of wine into a command not to get drunk.
b: The Greek verse goes on: "For if you give your eyes to the bowls and cups, afterward you will walk about more naked than a pestle" (see the variants on the next two lines). Its first words, mē methuskesthe oinō, are word for word the start of Ephesians 5:18: "Do not get drunk on wine, which only wastes your life. Be filled with the Spirit instead." Paul, who usually quotes the Greek Old Testament, may be echoing this verse.

p: The written Hebrew has 'in the purse'; the reading tradition has 'in the cup'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Qere; all ancient versions
readings.en: in the cup
readings.plain: in the cup

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Ketiv (the written consonants)
readings.en: in the purse (bag)
readings.plain: in the purse

why: 'Cup' fits the picture of wine sparkling. The Ketiv kis may be a spelling slip, or a wry joke: the wine winks at your purse.

a: as it shows its gleam in the cup
p: The Greek's second line warns against giving your eyes to the bowls and cups.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate
readings.en: when it gives its eye (sparkle) in the cup
readings.plain: as it shows its gleam in the cup

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.orig: ἐὰν γὰρ εἰς τὰς φιάλας καὶ τὰ ποτήρια δῷς τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς σου
readings.en: for if you give your eyes to the bowls and the cups
readings.plain: for if you fix your eyes on the bowls and the cups,

why: In the Hebrew the wine 'gives its eye', its sparkle; the Greek made the drinker the one who gives his eyes, a small change of reference with the same words.

p: Where the Hebrew says the wine goes down smoothly, the Greek warns that the drinker will end up naked.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate (ingreditur blande)
readings.en: it goes along smoothly
readings.plain: and slides down so easily

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.en: afterward you will walk about more naked than a pestle
readings.plain: afterward you will walk about more naked than a pestle.

why: The Hebrew is clear. The Greek may have read the verb 'walk' (yithallekh) as addressed to the drinker and supplied an image of ruin: a pestle is worn smooth and bare.

a: Strength is in a wise man
t: Strong, or stronger than the strong?
p: The Hebrew says a wise man is 'in strength'; the Greek says he is better than a strong man.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a wise man is in strength
readings.plain: Strength is in a wise man

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees; implies Hebrew מֵעָז ('than the strong'); followed by the NRSV and other modern versions
readings.en: a wise man is better than a strong one
readings.plain: A wise man is better than a strong one

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands, and 24:6 follows from it. The Greek reading fits the comparison style of Proverbs (16:32; 21:22) and needs only a small change of letters (ב for מ), so many scholars prefer it; the evidence is evenly balanced.
b: The Greek second line also differs: "and a man who has understanding is better than a large farm." That shows the Greek translator was comparing throughout, either because his Hebrew read that way or because he made it so.

a: He who guards your life knows
t: The one who guards, or the one who formed?
p: The Hebrew has 'the one who guards your life'; the Greek has 'the one who formed breath in all'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate (servatorem animae tuae)
readings.en: and the one who guards your life, he knows
readings.plain: He who guards your life knows

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees; probably reading יֹצֵר, 'who forms', for נֹצֵר
readings.orig: καὶ ὁ πλάσας πνοὴν πᾶσιν αὐτὸς οἶδεν πάντα
readings.en: and he who formed breath for all, he knows all things
readings.plain: He who formed the breath in everyone knows all things

why: The Hebrew 'guards' fits the line's play on life and death: the one who keeps your life knows whether you let others lose theirs. The Greek probably read a different first letter (י for נ), a common confusion, and thought of God as creator (Genesis 2:7).
b: The Greek also renders the excuse in the first line as "I do not know this one" (Ouk oida touton), as if the speaker denied knowing the condemned man (see the note).

p: The written Hebrew has 'your enemies'; the reading tradition has 'your enemy', which matches 'he' later in the verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Qere; Greek (ὁ ἐχθρός σου); Latin Vulgate (inimicus tuus)
readings.en: your enemy
readings.plain: When your enemy falls

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), Ketiv (the written consonants)
readings.en: your enemies
readings.plain: When your enemies fall

why: The singular matches 'when he trips' in the second line and is the reading of all the ancient versions. The Ketiv adds one letter (yod), probably by a copying slip.

a: Have nothing to do with people who want things changed.
p: The Hebrew warns against 'those who change'; the Greek reads 'do not disobey either of them'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: with those who change do not get involved
readings.plain: Have nothing to do with people who want things changed.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.en: and do not disobey either of them
readings.plain: Do not defy either one of them.

why: The Hebrew shonim, 'those who change', is unusual but makes sense of political rebels or those who 'think otherwise' (the KJV's 'them that are given to change'). The Greek seems to have read shneihem, 'the two of them', the word that appears in 24:22, and rewritten the line around it.
b: Readers of the Hebrew differ on shonim: people who change sides, those who seek political change (rebels), or those who are different (the Vulgate has detractoribus, 'slanderers'). Some modern scholars follow the Greek. In every reading the verse ties loyalty to God with loyalty to the king.

a: and who knows what ruin the two of them can bring?
t: Five extra couplets in the Greek
p: After 24:22 the Greek adds five couplets on the son who keeps the word and the king's deadly tongue.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate
readings.en: and the ruin of the two of them, who knows?
readings.plain: and who knows what ruin the two of them can bring?

readings.w: Old Greek (Rahlfs 24:22a–e; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus in Swete's notes)
readings.orig: λόγον φυλασσόμενος υἱὸς ἀπωλείας ἐκτὸς ἔσται... μάχαιρα γλῶσσα βασιλέως καὶ οὐ σαρκίνη
readings.en: a son who keeps the word will be free from ruin... a king's tongue is a sword, and not of flesh
readings.plain: and who knows what ruin the two of them can bring? / A son who keeps the word will stay clear of ruin, / for he took it and welcomed it. / Let no lie be spoken to a king, / and let no lie go out from his tongue. / A king's tongue is a sword, and not one of flesh; / whoever is handed over to it is crushed. / For if his anger is sharpened, / he destroys people, sinews and all, / and gnaws their bones and burns them like a flame, / so that they are not food even for eagles' chicks.

why: The added couplets are not in any Hebrew manuscript. They expand the warning of 24:21–22 about the king and are one of many Greek additions in Proverbs; most scholars think they were added by the translator or come from a Hebrew text that circulated more widely.

a: These too are by the wise:
t: By the wise, or to the wise?
p: The Hebrew heading says these sayings belong to the wise; the Greek has the teacher speak to the wise.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Latin Vulgate (haec quoque sapientibus)
readings.en: these also belong to the wise
readings.plain: These too are by the wise:

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), Rahlfs edition; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition agrees
readings.orig: ταῦτα δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν τοῖς σοφοῖς ἐπιγινώσκειν
readings.en: these things I say to you, the wise, to recognize
readings.plain: I say these things to you who are wise, for you to take note:

why: The Hebrew lachakhamim can mean 'by' or 'for' the wise. Read with 22:17 ('the words of the wise') it is a heading naming the authors. The Greek took it as 'to the wise' and made it a teacher's address.
b: In the Greek this heading does not follow 24:22 at all. It comes after the words of Agur (30:1–14), so that the sayings 24:23–34 sit between two halves of chapter 30 (see the note and the chapter page). In Swete's notes, Codex Sinaiticus also leaves out the next line, about favoring faces in court.
